summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ , a man with secondary progressive multiple sclerosis and prior cervical laminectomies, was admitted due to acute inability to walk, which had worsened over several days. He presented with severe leg spasticity, loss of proprioception, and urinary incontinence due to immobility. Evaluation revealed a urinary tract infection caused by Enterococcus, confirmed by urine culture, and pre-renal azotemia from dehydration, with improvement after IV fluids. An MS flare was suspected as the primary cause of neurological decline, likely triggered by the infection and dehydration. He was treated with a three-day course of IV methylprednisolone, IV ampicillin for the infection, and an increase in Tizanidine to 4 mg three times daily for spasticity. A drop in hematocrit was noted but attributed to IV fluid resuscitation and a likely small thigh hematoma, with no active bleeding found on CT. The cervical spine MRI was limited by motion artifact but showed no cord compression. He stabilized and was discharged to an extended care facility for rehabilitation with a plan to complete IV antibiotics and continue optimized spasticity management.
